content:
Use your church's approved values as the starting point for its public identity. A logo belongs within that identity, alongside the words, colors and type your team uses to communicate.

Give volunteers and designers a shared reference for those choices. A practical style guide can help them use the same visual elements and voice across your church's materials.

---

## Start with the values you already teach

Return to Defining Your Church Values before choosing artwork. It distinguishes foundational pillars from operating values, distinctives and lived culture. Bring your church's existing statements into the design conversation, and describe what those commitments look like in practice.

Use those statements to assess proposed wording. The values article asks you to describe what you actually are and do. If a proposed tagline introduces a new commitment, return it to your leaders for a values discussion before treating it as approved copy.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"A good name is to be chosen over great wealth, Favor is better than silver and gold."* — Proverbs 22:1 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Give the designer a clear brief

Write down the project before commissioning it. A design brief usually names the audience, goals, scope, budget, timeline and deliverables. Adapt those categories to your church.

Describe who you hope to reach and what the design needs to communicate. List the work you are requesting, such as a logo and a guide for using it. Agree on the budget and schedule with the designer before work begins.

Follow the responsibilities described in Promotion Leader Role. Have the Promotion Leader coordinate creative partners under the Senior Pastor's leadership, manage review and approval, and ensure the deliverables meet standards.

---

## Check names and marks before committing

The USPTO explains that a trademark can identify the source of goods or services through words, symbols or designs. Federal registration is optional and offers broader protection than an unregistered mark. Discuss your church's circumstances with a qualified trademark attorney rather than assuming every church must register.

Search for confusingly similar marks used with the same or related goods or services. The USPTO recommends checking federal registrations and pending applications, and common-law use. Its clearance guidance also lists state trademark and business registries, domain registries and internet searches.

Treat that research as a search for conflicts, not a promise of clearance. A trademark attorney can interpret results and advise on federal registration.

<Callout type="important">
Trademark guidance checked October 16, 2026. Confirm current guidance with the USPTO and an attorney before relying on it for your church's name or logo. This overview is general information, not legal advice.
</Callout>

---

## Review the logo in the places you will use it

Ask the designer to show the logo in your actual digital and printed materials. Adobe's logo guidance recommends checking how a design functions across different environments and sizes. Include a small mobile use and a large sign in that review.

Consider a full church-name version and a simpler version for tight spaces. Check a single-color treatment too, as a practical test of visual complexity. Have the designer explain when to use each approved version.

Document the smallest readable size and the empty space around the logo. Stanford's identity guide illustrates both kinds of rules. Set specifications for your own artwork rather than borrowing another organization's measurements.

<Callout type="warning">
Check the license before using stock artwork in a logo. Adobe Stock, for example, says its images cannot be used in or as a logo. A license for other promotional uses does not establish permission for that use.
</Callout>

---

## Keep the tagline faithful and clear

Use the tagline to express what you want people to know in your church's voice. Adobe's brand-guide advice describes a tagline as a quick expression of value. Work from the commitments already approved by your church.

Use the Promotion Leader article's emphasis on clarity and authentic messaging. Ask whether a guest would understand the proposed words and whether they describe the church truthfully. Bring unclear or inflated wording back for revision.

Record the approved wording and show how it appears with the church name. If the design combines the tagline and logo, have the designer provide instructions for using that combination and the separate elements.

---

## Choose colors and type people can read

Record digital color values and the printer's color specifications in the guide. Stanford's color guidance distinguishes digital RGB or HEX values from print color specifications. Give each supplier the values appropriate to the work.

Check the contrast between ordinary text and its background, including text placed over photographs. W3C's accessibility guidance recommends sufficient contrast and warns against using color alone to convey information. Apply those checks to invitations and website content, rather than assuming a brand color works for every purpose.

Specify readable text sizes, spacing and type styles. USWDS explains how these affect readability and advises against long passages of bold, italic or uppercase text. Show headings and body copy in a sample layout so volunteers can follow the chosen treatment.

---

## Make the style guide easy to use

Organize the decisions as instructions and examples. Use this outline as a working checklist for your own guide.

| Part | What to include |
|---|---|
| Church identity | Existing values and approved public wording |
| Logo | Approved versions, spacing, size and examples of misuse |
| Color | Digital values and print specifications |
| Type | Heading and body styles with readable spacing |
| Files | Clearly identified logo files for the intended uses |

Ask for a vector master as part of the agreed deliverables. SVG is a vector format that can scale without losing image quality. Request transparent PNG exports for digital uses that need them; PNG supports transparent backgrounds.

---

## Hand off the files with examples

Have the Promotion Leader review the completed work against the brief and coordinate any corrections with the designer. Give volunteers and suppliers the guide alongside the approved artwork. Stanford's logo guidance explicitly recommends sharing design resources with vendors.

Include examples of the materials your team will produce, using the agreed logo, colors and type. For website examples, check narrow screens as well as wider ones. W3C recommends considering different viewport sizes and keeping text readable as the available space changes.

<Callout type="tip">
Test the logo at the sizes and in the materials you plan to use. If it becomes unreadable, return to the designer for a suitable version before approving that application.
</Callout>
excerpt: Use your church's approved values to brief a designer, check names and logos, and create a style guide volunteers can follow.
title: Building Your Church's Brand: Logo, Tagline and Style Guide
